events.note: Plan approved for an outer breakwater roughly a mile long
Octagonal iron pierhead beacon replaced a wooden beacon
Red light of the pierhead beacon screened off on 13 Sept 1880
Iron pierhead beacon moved onto a 35-foot-square crib at the breakwater end, 17 Oct 1881
Iron breakwater tower changed from brown to white (Sept 1900)
Breakwater light renamed Oswego Light Station (15 Apr 1917)
Breakwater light electrified; Commissioner list of fiscal 1921 improvements
Iron breakwater tower discontinued 10 Aug 1931; temporary light the same day
Metal lighthouse on a crib at the end of the extended west breakwater
Fourth-order Fresnel lens (original)
Electric tyfon fog signal
Radiobeacon activated 25 Apr 1936, synchronized with the fog signal
Storm on Lake Ontario, 4 Dec 1942
Coast Guard picket boat capsized and was smashed on the breakwater, 4 Dec 1942; six men died
Coast Guard personnel withdrawn
Fresnel lens removed when the light was converted to solar power; placed on display at the museum
NRHP reference 00001468; NPS record dated 1 Dec 2000
City of Oswego received the deed (May 2009)
3 July 1914: Keeper Tucker brought two women, rescued from drowning by his son and two other young men, to the light station

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station record gives 1880 for the first light and a 1880 tower. The 1880 date belongs to the iron pierhead beacon: the red light was screened in Sept 1880 and the beacon moved onto a crib in Oct 1881. The present tower is 1934 (USLHS and LighthouseFriends).
LighthouseFriends dates his appointment as head keeper at Oswego to 1929; the USLHS roster starts his stint in 1934. The story gives both dates and does not choose.

The county release gives eight Coast Guardsmen besides Wilson, four reaching the breakwater, and says the crew relieved Jackson before the boat capsized. LighthouseFriends gives seven besides Wilson, two reaching the breakwater, and says Jackson was taken aboard when the waves hit the crib. Both give six dead. The story gives both accounts.

corrections.proposed: tower, built 1934, metal, standing; 1877/1881 iron pierhead beacon discontinued 1931
corrections.why: The standing light is the 1934 metal tower (USLHS: year tower established 1934; LighthouseFriends). The 1880 date belongs to the iron pierhead beacon, which LighthouseFriends says was discontinued in 1931. The 12.0 m figure is not matched to any source read.
The present light's year established is 1934 (USLHS). The 1880 date belongs to the iron pierhead beacon's red light, screened in Sept 1880 (LighthouseFriends).

notes_for_editor: 1) The NRHP nomination PDF (npgallery 00001468) is the 22 KB 'not yet digitized' placeholder, so the nomination was not read; the NRHP date comes from the NPGallery asset record only (Date Published 12/1/2000; significant year 1934). 2) The USLHS place record's coordinates are about 45 km from the station's record position; the roster was matched by name; the record's 1934 date and optic data match the 1934 light. 3) Wikipedia dates the breakwater light to 1889; no source read supports it, so it is not used. 4) Which tower Charles H. Tucker kept before 1917 is unresolved. LighthouseFriends lists him as assistant at the breakwater light (1896-1897) and head keeper of the stone tower (1904-1929). The 1914 Bulletin calls him keeper of 'Oswego Light Station'. The fiscal 1918 table of assists names him at 'Oswego Light Station, N. Y.' (not a list of keepers, as first drafted). He is not given other_stations because no source ties him to a separate station record. The fiscal 1915 assists table (Commissioner volume, scan p.68, printed p.63) has a 'C. H. Tucker, keeper, Oswego' entry that the OCR runs into the vessel column ('Row boat'); it is not used, and the page image should be checked before any use. 5) LighthouseFriends' Keepers (Main) list includes Florence G. Garland (1903), a woman head keeper of the stone tower. The story names her in the keepers section; she is not on this roster because her post was the stone tower, not the breakwater light. Check before any change. 6) The 1887-1917 breakwater roster lines come from LighthouseFriends alone, spelled as it prints them, and have not been checked against a primary keeper register (NARA registers, Commissioner reports). The USLHS place record has no entries before 1934 for this light. 7) 1942 accident: sources disagree on numbers and sequence (see resolved_conflicts). The county calls Jackson a Boatswain's Mate First Class and names the commanding officer 'Alston Wilson' (it prints 'Altson' once). The story uses 'Alston Wilson' with no middle initial, because no source read gives one. The archive lists Jackson as first assistant keeper; both are given. 8) Chronicling America returned no hits for 'Oswego breakwater' 1880-1900 or for Oswego keepers in 1942; the 1942 accident rests on the county release and LighthouseFriends. 9) The Coast Guard Atlantic Area station history page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. 10) Other Tucker entries not used: the 1912-1917 Bulletin index lists 'Tucker, Charles H., keeper Oswego light station, rescue 132' (the July 1914 rescue); the 1918-1923 index lists 'Tucker, Charles H., keeper Oswego Harbor, rescue 36', which has not been read. 11) Lighthouse Board reports for 1880-1890 are not in the local corpus; the 1880-81 events rest on LighthouseFriends. 12) Tours: LighthouseFriends' visitor information is undated (Fridays and Saturdays, mid-June to early September). The county's 2022 release mentions educational lighthouse tours. Current arrangements are unconfirmed. 13) Lens: LighthouseFriends says the fourth-order lens is in the museum; not confirmed in person. 14) Karl H. Jackson's middle initial: USLHS and LighthouseFriends give H; a social-media post gives A, not used. 15) Light and fog signal, unresolved: LighthouseFriends (1934 description) gives a flashing red light and an electric tyfon fog signal; the Lighthouse Service Bulletin of 1935 (PDF p.29) gives an occulting red light of 5,100 candlepower and an air horn. The story states both and does not choose. 16) Keepers' quarters: LighthouseFriends dates the duplex at 31 W. Fifth Street to 1934; the USLHS record gives 1936 for keeper's quarters attached to the tower. The two may be different buildings; not reconciled. 17) The 1935 Bulletin's crib and superstructure description (timber crib 50 feet square; steel building with square tower at the northeast corner) differs in detail from LighthouseFriends' metal lighthouse; not used. 18) Newspapers cited second-hand by LighthouseFriends (Oswego Palladium-Times 1907, 1931, 1938, 1942) were not read directly. 19) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the quotes from the 1893 and 1894 Board reports were checked on the Internet Archive text (1893 passage in the fiscal 1893 report, scan p.199; 1894 passage in the fiscal 1894 report, scan p.499). The 1914 Bulletin rescue (PDF p.36) and the 1935 Bulletin passage (PDF p.29) were checked on the PDF text.
